title: Pixels over Symbols: Sensory Realism Improves Behavioral Alignment in Models of Cognition
claim: Compare humans, abstract-input models, and vision-language models on identical tasks, then measure how consistent their behavior is with humans'.
layout: 3 columns (Inputs, Agents, Behavioral Analyses), 3 rows, left-to-right flow
description: A wide schematic with three column headers in bold italic: Inputs, Agents and Behavioral Analyses. The left Inputs column has three dotted-line-separated rows. Task Indicator shows a text prompt and a 43-dimensional task vector drawn as segmented bars. Natural Stimuli shows two grayscale photos, a car and a face, with a 500ms delay between them. Abstract Stimuli shows one-hot bars for category, identity and position, plus scalar inputs for rotation and object size, with small colored shape icons. The middle column has three rows: a brain-in-head icon for humans, a network graph sphere for RNN models, and a robot-chip icon for vision-language models. Each agent receives stimulus images plus text or task symbols. Dotted arrows lead to the right column. Each row there shows a Match/Non-Match response, a 3D tensor of tasks, trials and subjects or models, correlation r(...) between probability bars, and a red-blue consistency matrix. The eye goes first to the colorful agents and heatmaps.
caption: Schematic of the Experimental Setup. Models receive both task and stimulus information in their inputs. Task indicator is provided in either textual or one-hot while stimuli are presented in their naturalistic or abstract formats. In the abstract format, information about the primary object in the scene is provided as a combination of one-hot (category, object identity, position) and scalar values. Three groups are studied: humans, neural network models trained on abstract or natural inputs, and pretrained vision-language models. Behavioral responses are collected from each group and used to estimate the choice probabilities for each task trial. These probabilities are then used to calculate behavioral consistency with humans using different metrics.
abstract: Computational models of cognition have traditionally relied on abstract symbolic inputs that approximate sensory experiences with simplified vector representations. This simplification reflects historical computational constraints and a long-held assumption that the details of sensory realism are incidental to the study of cognitive processes. Recent advances have enabled the development of sensory-realistic models capable of performing diverse cognitive tasks, yet whether sensory realism meaningfully shapes cognition has not been formally established. We address this gap through a large-scale empirical comparison of abstract and sensory-realistic neural network models trained on a battery of memory-dependent decision-making tasks. Our results show that sensory-realistic models mirror human behavioral response patterns significantly more than their abstract counterparts, though a substantial gap to human internal behavioral consistency remains even for the best tested models. By analyzing the internal dynamics of these systems, we find that the learned recurrent weights are not the main source of this divergence. In fact, frozen abstract-trained weights driven by sensory-realistic inputs recover the human consistency of sensory-realistic models. The resulting dynamics are also within the seed-to-seed variability of sensory-realistic models. Together, our findings argue that across a broad set of visual working-memory tasks, sensory realism accounts for a substantial portion of the model-human behavioral agreement, more than the choice of sequence architecture and comparable to the choice of vision encoder. These results suggest that findings obtained from abstract task models in neuroscience should be more carefully interpreted in light of their potential behavioral limitations.
